extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance on what constitutes genuine poetry, with emphasis on unity of effect, appropriate length (especially for 'minor' or short poems), and the relation of poetic merit to emotional elevation rather than didactic truth or mere bulk. Includes examples and anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: A long poem does not exist / brevity as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: I hold that a long poem does not exist. The phrase, 'a long poem,' is simply a flat contradiction in terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem deserves its title only insofar as it excites by elevating the soul; that elevating excitement is transient and cannot be sustained throughout a composition of any great length. After at most half an hour the excitement flags; therefore true poetry must be of limited extent. Example/argument: even great epics (e.g., 'Paradise Lost') can only be regarded as a series of minor poems if judged poetically throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity / totality of effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem's value depends on its Unity — its totality of effect or impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is the vital requisite in all works of Art; when Unity is lost across length, the work alternates between passages of true poetry and platitude. A poem should be constructed to produce a single, sustained impression/effect (which constrains length). Practical consequence: long works risk being read as aggregated minor pieces rather than a single poetic whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic value measured by elevating excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem deserves its title only inasmuch as it excites, by elevating the soul. The value of the poem is in the ratio of this elevating excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poems by the degree to which they elevate the reader emotionally/spiritually, not by technicalities, length, or effort. The central test of poetic merit is its power to produce an elevating emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate length or sustained effort with merit
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent of a poetical work is, ceteris paribus, the measure of its merit is a proposition sufficiently absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should not praise a poem merely because it is long or required 'sustained effort.' Perseverance is distinct from genius. Judge works by the impression they make rather than the time or labor expended. (Targeted critique of periodical reviewers who laud 'sustained effort'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid undue brevity / epigrammatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Undue brevity degenerates into mere epigrammatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very short poems can produce brilliant or vivid effects but rarely a profound or enduring one; they may fail to 'stamp' deeply on the reader. There is a middle ground: poems should be concise enough to sustain a single effect but long enough to achieve depth ('steady pressing down of the stamp upon the wax'). Examples: some of De Beranger's and Shelley's short pieces are vivid yet too light to sink deeply into public attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Didacticism is a heresy for poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The heresy of 'The Didactic' assumes that the ultimate object of all Poetry is Truth and that every poem should inculcate a moral; this idea corrupts Poetical Literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should not be judged primarily as moral or instructive tract; making 'truth' or moral lesson the chief criterion of poetic merit is a mistaken approach. The essay criticizes especially contemporary (American/Bostonian) tendencies to prioritize didactic aims over poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reading/adaptation of long works (epics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great long poems may be regarded, for poetic appreciation, as a series of minor poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one wants to preserve Unity or the total poetic effect, long epics are best approached in parts (or read with selective omission) because sustained enthusiasm cannot be maintained continuously; re-reading and selective reading can alter one's judgment of passages. This is both a readerly strategy and an implicit admonition to poets about the risks of epic scope.
